analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for corporate bonuses over $1 million, including "performance-based" pay.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2017 and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal tax law already bars publicly traded companies from deducting executive pay above $1 million a year, but it carves out big exceptions: bonuses labeled "performance-based" and commissions can be deducted no matter how large. This bill would close those loopholes, extend the $1 million cap to former executives drawing deferred compensation, and apply the rule to every company that reports to the Securities and Exchange Commission. The practical effect: companies paying multimillion-dollar bonuses would owe more tax, and the Treasury would collect more revenue that otherwise subsidizes executive pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in two ways. First, every dollar of a public company's deductible executive bonus is income the company does not pay tax on, so other taxpayers pick up the difference; closing the loopholes means the companies, not the public, absorb that cost. Second, the Treasury would collect additional revenue that could fund public services or reduce deficits. Tax fairness groups have long argued the current exceptions let companies call almost any bonus "performance-based" and deduct it anyway.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the $1 million deduction cap to any current or former officer, director, or employee of a publicly held corporation, so retired executives' deferred payouts are covered too.
Eliminates the exceptions that currently let companies deduct commission-based pay and compensation tied to performance goals, closing the main escape hatches from the cap.
Applies the cap to every corporation registered with or reporting to the SEC, not just a narrower set of companies.
Directs the Treasury Secretary to write the rules and reporting requirements needed to enforce the cap, and sets the change to start with tax years beginning after 2017.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies and their highest-paid executives. Companies paying more than $1 million to any single executive would lose deductions for the excess, raising their tax bills — costs ultimately borne by shareholders through lower earnings or by executives through leaner pay packages if boards restructure compensation to avoid the tax.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the cost of doing business for publicly traded companies, which shareholders bear through lower after-tax earnings when companies keep pay structures unchanged.
Companies may simply restructure compensation rather than pay more tax, and the bill leaves detailed enforcement to Treasury regulations, adding compliance and rule-writing burdens.

Expanding the cap to former employees sweeps in deferred compensation arrangements that were negotiated under the old rules, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge falls on companies and retirees alike.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward tax fairness: today a public company can deduct almost unlimited bonuses simply by labeling them performance-based, and ordinary taxpayers effectively subsidize that. The costs fall on a specific, well-resourced group — public companies and top executives — rather than on workers or consumers directly. Companies would face higher tax bills and some compliance complexity, and some might restructure pay to game the new rules, but on balance the bill targets a narrow, lucrative loophole without touching wages or prices for most people.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 2017–2018 Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jack Reed introduced the bill on January 10, 2017, together with Senator Richard Blumenthal.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where its tax provisions would be considered.
Seven Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors.
The Finance Committee took no further action on the bill — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and it never reached the Senate floor during the 115th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded companies and their top executives keep the ability to deduct multimillion-dollar bonuses from their taxes, and the Treasury forgoes the revenue the bill would have raised.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to close the performance-based and commission pay deductions from the $1 million executive pay cap.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Joined Reed in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or hearing on the bill, so it never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded; support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor and all seven cosponsors — while the Republican-chaired Finance Committee simply never acted, so no Republican went on record either way.

industries.note: Today these companies deduct executive pay above $1 million whenever it is labeled performance-based or commission-based, lowering their tax bills at other taxpayers' expense; the bill ends that deduction, so the industry's financial interest in the status quo runs directly against the public's interest in not subsidizing executive bonuses.
Extending the cap to former officers and employees covers deferred and retirement payouts as well as current pay, which would pressure boards to trim or restructure multimillion-dollar packages.

The bill would hand the Treasury Secretary new authority to write reporting and enforcement rules for the cap, adding administrative work but also the tools to police executive compensation deductions.
